key_insight: Jev, a non-generative medical answer model, was fast and low-cost, but its performance was only competitive on PubMedQA and notably weaker on harder diagnostic benchmarks.
clinical_relevance: The findings suggest Jev may be useful for narrow, benchmarked medical QA tasks, but it should not be used clinically without task-specific validation, especially for diagnosis and unanswerable questions.
method: Evaluated Jev 1.13 on four medical benchmarks: MetaMedQA, PubMedQA, DiagnosisArena-MCQ, and NEJM Case Challenges.
Compared performance against GPT-6 Sol with and without medium reasoning.
Assessed top-1 accuracy, calibration, selective prediction, and recognition of unanswerable questions.
evidence_signal: Across 8,469 requests, Jev returned valid answers for all items, with accuracy ranging from 78.4% on PubMedQA to 59.8% on DiagnosisArena-MCQ and 61.8% on NEJM cases.
watch_item: Its confidence was not consistently reliable across tasks, and performance dropped sharply on examination-style and complex diagnostic cases, limiting real-world clinical deployment.
paper_title: Jev in Medicine: A Benchmark Evaluation. Preliminary Results
